entry.title: How abap2UI5 Complements RAP and Fiori Elements – Now Also as a Custom Control
entry.content:
With abap2UI5, a complete UI5 app is a single ABAP class – source code only, nothing else to create, generate or deploy. That gives a lot of freedom, and nothing is held back: the whole UI5 control library is available through XML views, built in ABAP. And under the hood, it is all standard technology: what runs in the browser is a normal UI5 freestyle app, and what runs on the server is plain ABAP on released APIs.

Which UI technology, and when?

Anyone who builds user interfaces on SAP knows the question. Classic screens or the newer UI technologies? And within the newer ones: RAP with Fiori Elements, Fiori Elements with developer extensibility, or a switch to UI5 freestyle? Each of these decisions is complex on its own, and every additional UI technology makes the landscape more complex, not less.

So where could abap2UI5 fit in?

Not a replacement – a complement

abap2UI5 is not here to replace any existing technology. The recommendation is simple: go with RAP and Fiori Elements as far as they take you. RAP is powerful: CDS views for the data model, a behavior definition for the business logic, a service binding, and with Fiori Elements on top a complete, consistent UI that SAP maintains – often with surprisingly little code. Where that fits, it is the right choice.

But there are places where a switch to abap2UI5 makes sense:

  • The data model does not map one to one onto a CDS model – the structure is only known at runtime, or the screen is a tool rather than a view on a business object.
  • The system runs on a release where RAP is not available yet.
  • A small screen is needed quickly – an admin tool, a correction screen, a dashboard for one team – and a full RAP stack would be more effort than the screen itself.
  • Developer extensibility has been reached, and the next step would otherwise be a UI5 freestyle app.

In those places abap2UI5 complements RAP and Fiori Elements. It does not compete with them – it is one more way to build a UI5 app, on the same technology. The best way to find out whether it fits: just try it.

Runs everywhere your ABAP runs

abap2UI5 runs on every release from NetWeaver 7.02 up to ABAP Cloud. The framework itself uses released APIs only, so it is ready for clean core – and whether an app is cloud-ready is decided by the app's own code, not by the framework.

Under the hood, abap2UI5 is nothing else than a normal UI5 freestyle app, ready to be deployed wherever UI5 apps run: on the ABAP system itself or on SAP BTP.

Open source, nothing to lose

abap2UI5 is open source under the MIT license. Trying it out costs nothing and does not bite. And if it does not fit, it can simply be deleted again, or just left unused.

How to start

Install abap2UI5 with abapGit in a few minutes – everything needed is in the installation guide.

Then there are several ways to develop:

  • Start in the browser. The abap2UI5 playground runs abap2UI5 entirely in the browser – no system needed. Write the first app there, get familiar with the basic behavior, then copy the class into the system and run it there. In a second step, add the business logic – and the first working app is done.
  • Design the screen first. For those who prefer visual screen design, the new layout designer is there to try: build the screen the way it should look, copy the app into the system and keep developing.
  • Learn from samples. The sample catalog has hundreds of ready-to-run apps, searchable by control and by UI5 release.

There is no vendor lock-in: an abap2UI5 app is pure ABAP code, in your own system, transportable like any other class – and easy to share with others.

Into production, next to your other apps

A finished app goes into production like any other: integrated into the SAP Fiori launchpad or SAP Build Work Zone as a tile. There, abap2UI5 apps live right next to your RAP and UI5 freestyle apps, and no end user sees a difference – because under the hood an abap2UI5 app is nothing else than a normal UI5 app.

New: abap2UI5 as a custom control

abap2UI5 does not only run as a full app. It now also comes wrapped in a UI5 custom control, which brings it right into the apps you already have: into a UI5 freestyle app, into a Fiori Elements app, and into the developer extensions of Fiori Elements – custom sections and custom pages.

 This fits the path a new app typically follows today:

  1. Start with RAP. CDS view entities, a behavior definition with validations, determinations and draft handling, a service binding, and a Fiori Elements app with list report and object page. As long as the annotations can express what is needed, stay here.
  2. When the backend cannot go further, use developer extensibility. Sooner or later a requirement comes along that the annotations have no word for – a credit check for one sales order that needs three function modules and a decision table, or a delivery simulation with a chart. Then the next step is a frontend project for the Fiori Elements app (for example with SAP Fiori tools) and its well-defined extension points: custom columns, custom actions, custom sections and custom pages. The list report, the object page, the draft handling and the navigation all stay where they are.
  3. Put abap2UI5 into the custom section. What used to go into such an extension was an XML fragment, a controller and JavaScript. Now the section can hold the abap2UI5 control instead – and its content is an ABAP class.

The control is z2ui5.embed.Container from the npm package @abap2ui5/embed-control.

One fragment, one class

A custom section is an entry in manifest.json (SAP Fiori tools generates it via the Page Map):

"SalesOrderObjectPage": {
  "type": "Component",
  "name": "sap.fe.templates.ObjectPage",
  "options": {
    "settings": {
      "contextPath": "/SalesOrder",
      "content": {
        "body": {
          "sections": {
            "creditCheck": {
              "template": "sales.order.ext.CreditCheck",
              "title": "Credit Check",
              "position": { "placement": "After", "anchor": "General" }
            }
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

and a fragment, which holds the control, bound to the sales order on the page:

<core:FragmentDefinition
    xmlns:core="sap.ui.core"
    xmlns:z2ui5="z2ui5.embed">
    <z2ui5:Container
        core:require="{ Section: 'sales/order/ext/CreditCheck' }"
        app="{ path: 'SalesOrder', formatter: 'Section.app' }"
        params="{ path: 'SalesOrder', targetType: 'any', formatter: 'Section.params' }"
        height="420px"/>
</core:FragmentDefinition>

Two small formatters decide which ABAP class runs and what it gets:

sap.ui.define([], () => {
  "use strict";

  return {
    app(order) {
      return order ? "ZCL_SALES_ORDER_CREDIT_CHECK" : "";
    },

    params(order) {
      return order ? { salesorder: order } : null;
    },
  };
});

That is all the JavaScript there is, and it does not grow: whatever the section does next is written in the class. Nothing starts before the page has an order, and navigating to the next order ends the running abap2UI5 session and starts a new one with the new number.

(targetType: 'any' is needed with OData V4: without it, the binding tries to convert the Edm.String key into the object type of params and fails.)

Importing parameters, e.g. the sales order

On the ABAP side the values arrive as startup parameters – think of them as the app's IMPORTING parameters. client->get( )-t_comp_params is a table of name and value, read once when the app starts:

METHOD z2ui5_if_app~main.

  IF client->check_on_init( ).
    LOOP AT client->get( )-t_comp_params INTO DATA(param).
      IF to_lower( param-n ) = `salesorder`.
        sales_order = param-v.
      ENDIF.
    ENDLOOP.
    " read the order, run the check, build the view
  ENDIF.

ENDMETHOD.

Every value arrives as a string, and any number of them can be handed over: the order number, the sold-to party, the sales organization. From there it is an ordinary abap2UI5 app. It reads the order with a SELECT, or through the RAP business object with EML – and then the validations, the draft and the authorizations of the business object still apply. The business logic stays in RAP; abap2UI5 only puts a different UI in front of it, for this one section.

Several apps side by side

Every control runs its own abap2UI5 session. Two sections with two containers are two apps with two independent states – a credit check and a delivery simulation for the same order, each a class of its own, each started with the same order number:

<z2ui5:Container app="ZCL_SALES_ORDER_CREDIT_CHECK" params="{ ... }" height="420px"/>
<z2ui5:Container app="ZCL_SALES_ORDER_DELIVERY_SIM" params="{ ... }" height="420px"/>

The same goes for a custom page: a view of its own in the app's routing, with as many containers as the page needs.

And in UI5 freestyle?

The control is an ordinary UI5 control, so it works in any freestyle app as well:

<mvc:View xmlns:mvc="sap.ui.core.mvc" xmlns:z2ui5="z2ui5.embed">
  <z2ui5:Container app="Z2UI5_CL_UI5_APP_HI_WORLD" height="400px"/>
</mvc:View>

An existing freestyle app can take over individual screens or areas written in ABAP, without being rebuilt.

What it takes

In the UI5 or Fiori Elements app, three entries:

1. The dependency: npm install @abap2ui5/embed-control

2. ui5.yaml, so that ui5 build takes the control along:

builder:
  settings:
    includeDependency:
      - "@abap2ui5/embed-control"

3. manifest.json, the resource root of the control's namespace:

"sap.ui5": {
  "resourceRoots": { "z2ui5.embed": "./thirdparty/z2ui5/embed/" }
}

What it does not take: no launchpad target mapping, no controller extension, and no copy of the abap2UI5 frontend in the app. The control loads the frontend from the abap2UI5 service it talks to anyway (/sap/bc/z2ui5?z2ui5-bundle), so the frontend always has exactly the version of the backend.

On the system, abap2UI5 1.146.0 or later is needed. From that release on, an embedded abap2UI5 leaves the URL hash to the page it runs in, so the object page stays an object page after a roundtrip. The page and the abap2UI5 service have to share an origin, which is the case for every app deployed to the same system or routed through an approuter. The control supports UI5 1.71 and later, the same floor as abap2UI5 itself. Fiori Elements apps for OData V2 work the same way, with the control in an object page extension instead of a custom section.

Try it

  • The control: abap2UI5/embed-control, published on npm as @abap2ui5/embed-control
  • The examples: abap2UI5/samples-embed-control – a UI5 freestyle app, Fiori Elements apps for OData V4 and V2 with two abap2UI5 apps side by side on the object page, and a UI Integration Card for SAP Build Work Zone. They also run locally without an SAP system.
  • One abapGit pull: the branch rap installs a complete example on an S/4HANA system (2020 or later): a RAP service, a Fiori Elements app as BSP, and the abap2UI5 classes it starts from the object page.
  • The documentation: Fiori Elements Integration

Summary

RAP and Fiori Elements come first: RAP for the business logic, Fiori Elements for the standard UI, developer extensibility when the annotations cannot go further, and UI5 freestyle where the browser really has to be smart. These are great technologies, and they stay exactly where they are.

abap2UI5 is a complement to them – as a full app where a quick ABAP-only screen is the better fit, and now as a custom control right inside the apps you already run. No end user sees a difference, no vendor lock-in is added, and trying it costs nothing.

Which screen in your landscape would you rather write in plain ABAP? Share your thoughts in the comments. Feedback, issues and pull requests are always welcome on GitHub.

The whole project is developed by ABAP enthusiasts who share their knowledge and time – big kudos to all contributors to abap2UI5. Join the ABAP open source community and work with us.

Happy ABAPing! 🦖🦕🦣

entry.title: Agentic ABAP with MCP: what is really solving problems for you?
entry.content:
With the major update of the ABAP development tools MCP server, MCP for ABAP is no longer an experiment. It now works with Claude Code, Copilot, Codex and the other CLI tools, and many of us already use some kind of agent in daily ABAP work.

I have been building and using agents on top of the ADT REST API for a few months, in my own S/4HANA 2023 lab. Instead of another how-to, I would like to open a discussion: where does it really help, where does it fail, and what could we share as a community? My notes first.

1. The first explanation is often plausible and wrong

This is true for people and for agents. A classic: SQL 305 on a CDS view, "single-row query returns more than one row". The usual explanation is a to-one association that finds duplicates. In my lab that alone gave no error: a LEFT OUTER MANY TO ONE JOIN from MARA to MAKT, for a material with 3 texts, returned 3 rows. The 305 only came with a scalar subquery that returned more than one row.

What I learned: wherever an explanation comes from, mine or the agent's, it gets reproduced in a sandbox before I believe it. The test is cheap, the wrong explanation is expensive.

2. Reading standard code is where it shines, if you know the limits

Following a call chain through the Gateway runtime classes, to see which DPC methods are really called, is a job of minutes for an agent and of an afternoon for me.

But tools can lie by silence. In my lab, the where-used list of /IWBEP/IF_MGW_CORE_SRV_RUNTIME showed one custom class and none of the SAP classes that I then saw using it in their source. And a text search across packages only covers what it really opened.

What I learned: an empty result is not proof that something doesn't exist. The agent must say what it did not search.

3. The system is the judge, but test the judge first

For code written by a model, I let the system decide: syntax check, ATC, ABAP Unit. Before trusting the judge, I give it two controls: the correct solution must pass, and a known mistake must fail (for example, the language condition in the WHERE instead of the ON of a text join). If the known mistake passes, "it compiles" is quietly becoming "it is right".

4. Context is the real cost

/IWBEP/CL_MGW_ABS_DATA alone has more than 8,000 lines of source. One whole read of a class like this fills a big part of the context, and everything after it gets slower and more expensive. In my own numbers, most of the cost was the model reading a big context again and again, not the answers it wrote. Reading one method, or searching first and reading after, is the habit that pays.

5. Human in the loop, by habit

Read only by default. Writes only in $TMP in my lab, and only after I say yes. Transports stay with a person. It is the same idea as the "safety by default" policy of the SAP server, and I think it is the right default for everybody.

What I would like to hear from you

  1. Which tasks really save you time today: investigation and reading, writing new objects, reviews, tests?
  2. Do you use the official ADT MCP server, a community server, or your own? What made you choose?
  3. How do you check what the agent tells you before you act on it?
  4. How do you deal with authorizations and transports when an agent can write?
  5. What would be worth sharing as a community: AGENTS.md patterns, prompts that work, or a set of "known hard" ABAP questions to test agents on?

If there is interest, I am happy to collect the answers in a follow-up.

entry.title: My ABAP Escaped the Server, Or: Everything Gets Better with Go.
entry.content:
Or: Everything Gets Better with Go.

TL;DR: ABAP report on ZX Spectrum, CP/M, MOS AgonLight (ez80), and a mac.

I like JavaScript, and TypeScript too. JavaScript has become something of a lingua franca of modern computing, rather like BASIC was in the eighties: back then you could walk up to almost any home computer and find a BASIC interpreter waiting for you, and although the machines were different, the dialects were different, and sometimes even the meaning of PRINT was a matter of local tradition, you could usually get something running. Today it's JavaScript — in browsers, servers, desktop applications, little embedded environments, and places where you might reasonably wonder who invited it.

I love being able to take an idea and run it almost anywhere, and TypeScript makes the whole arrangement much more comfortable once the idea grows beyond a few hundred lines. But I also love Go. There is something deeply satisfying about compiling a program into a native executable, copying that one file to another machine and watching it run, without a dependency installation ceremony, a carefully reconstructed development environment, or a server that must be started beforehand.

After spending the last couple of months getting ABAP to run outside SAP with Open SteamGate, I began to wonder whether we could go a little further. OSG could already run ABAP locally, serve OData, work with CDS and connect to Eclipse, and I wrote an entire article about how a simple experiment had grown into something resembling an application server.

But what if I didn't need an application server at all, and just wanted to run a report? A perfectly ordinary ABAP report, with PARAMETERS, SELECT-OPTIONS, a selection screen, some Open SQL, a little file processing and WRITE statements at the end. Could I compile it into an executable and run it in my terminal — not start a server, not install a runtime, not connect to a development system, just run the program, and preferably have it stop when it finishes?

Well, yes, as it turns out. And then the terminal started acquiring features. 😃

The report that acquired a terminal

Let me show you where this ended up.

This is an ABAP report compiled into a native executable by osabap, part of Open SteamGate's new ABAP-to-Go compiler. The report still has its PARAMETERS and SELECT-OPTIONS, its INITIALIZATION and START-OF-SELECTION events are still there, and WRITE still produces the output; but instead of opening a selection screen in SAP GUI, the program renders it as a form in the terminal, where you can move between fields, edit values, toggle checkboxes and execute the report. The source is ABAP, and the result is a native executable.

I rather like command-line tools, so the next thing I wanted was to run the same report without the interactive screen. Parameters become command-line options, a checkbox becomes a flag, and SELECT-OPTIONS can be given as repeated values or as ranges. WRITE output goes to stdout, messages go to stderr, and the process returns an exit status that another program can understand, so the report can sit in a shell pipeline, a scheduled job or a CI run.

A classic ABAP report had become a CLI tool. The funny thing is that the report itself doesn't need to know about any of this: we haven't rewritten its business logic in a special command-line language. The compiler takes the report and its supported dependencies, produces Go, and builds an executable that carries the runtime it needs, so neither Go nor Node is required on the machine that runs it — both belong to the build. This is a growing implementation of a supported ABAP subset, not a promise that every report from every SAP system will compile unchanged; but for the reports that do compile, it is a rather different way of deploying ABAP, and quite a pleasant way of running it.

Naturally, I pressed F4

Once the terminal selection screen worked, I started doing what an ABAP developer does with a selection screen, and almost immediately I pressed F4. Of course I did.

If a report asks for a filename, you don't really want to type the whole path into a terminal field, and ABAP already has a perfectly good way of offering values for a field: AT SELECTION-SCREEN ON VALUE-REQUEST. So why not let it work in the terminal too?

And there it is. The terminal form calls the report's value-request event; when the report uses one of the supported frontend file dialogs, the terminal opens a file browser, you move with the arrow keys, filter with /, choose with Enter, and the chosen path goes back into the ABAP parameter as though this were a perfectly normal thing for it to do. The same machinery covers the file-open, file-save and directory-browse calls of CL_GUI_FRONTEND_SERVICES, within the supported terminal implementation.

There was one rather important question, though: now that the report could browse files on my computer, which files should it be allowed to see? The answer is only the directories explicitly granted to it, with reading and writing granted separately. The browser lists the permitted roots, and the DATASET implementation applies the same sandbox when the ABAP code actually opens a file, including paths it constructs without the browser. A file chooser that politely hides a forbidden directory is not much of a security boundary if OPEN DATASET can simply read it anyway, so F4 didn't just need a pretty interface; it needed to agree with the file-access rules underneath it.

 

The result is a native terminal application whose user interface is still described by an ABAP report. You can even serve the selection screen to a real SAP GUI over a local DIAG connection, although that is a separate, limited frontend mode, and the terminal F4 browser belongs to the terminal form, not to it.

So we started with a command-line executable, and it had now acquired a selection screen, value help, a SQLite database when the report has tables of its own, and access to files under explicit permissions. This was beginning to feel familiar. Fortunately, it could still exit when the report finished, which was becoming an important design feature.

The implementation and examples are described in osabap, and the F4 implementation has its own documentation.

But how did ABAP become Go?

The nice thing about working on top of Lars Hvam Petersen's abaplint ecosystem is that we didn't have to start by teaching a new parser the ABAP language: abaplint already understands an extraordinary amount of ABAP syntax and structure, and its transpiler already handles expression precedence and many of the language's complications. I wanted to reuse that knowledge rather than reproduce it, and at first the idea sounded like simply adding another backend: where the existing transpiler produces JavaScript, ours would produce Go.

This is easier to say than to do. JavaScript, Go and ABAP have rather different ideas about values, types and operations, and you cannot translate a method call into a Go method call and hope that everything around it behaves correctly. In ABAP the receiving type can decide how an expression is evaluated, so computing with the obvious Go types and converting the answer afterwards may already be the wrong calculation; moving values between structures has its own semantics; internal tables are not quite slices; references and method-local data have lifetimes that don't map neatly onto Go declarations; and, of course, there is SY, because there always is.

So the interesting part became the layer in between: a typed intermediate representation, or IR, in which the frontend has already decided what each operation means. The calculation type is known and conversions are explicit, so the backend doesn't look at an expression and improvise an interpretation of ABAP — it expresses a decision that has already been made. The path is roughly:

ABAP → abaplint parser → typed IR → Go → native executable

The frontend reuses abaplint’s parser and the transpiler’s precedence pass, then makes every ABAP decision once, in gogen’s typed IR. Two emitters spell that IR as Go or as JavaScript. From Go come two kinds of program: one report as a native command, or OSGo, open-steamgate’s own ABAP runtime compiled into one server binary.

Sources: tools/gogen/README.md “Shape” and “Language or model?”, docs/osabap-native.md, docs/osgo-release.md (“OSGo does not serve ADT yet”).

The generated Go uses a runtime library for the ABAP behaviours that don't belong to Go's language model, such as internal tables, conversion rules and session state. Once we had this representation, we could test it against the original ABAP behaviour, including recordings from a real SAP system, which mattered, because a compiler that produces a wrong answer very quickly has not improved the situation very much.

I would love to say that we got every rule right on the first attempt. We did not. Some of the differences were small enough to fit in the last bit of a floating-point value, and others were visible in whole frames of an animation: you might remember the mountains and the rotating tesseract from the previous article, and drawing the output turned out to be a remarkably effective way of noticing when two runtimes disagreed about arithmetic. Once the Go backend produced correct results for the tested subset, we started measuring.

Everything gets better with Go. Or does it?

The first numbers were encouraging. On a recursive Fibonacci workload the generated Go took about 0.24 ms, against roughly 24 ms through the existing transpiled JavaScript — about a hundred times faster — and a million-row internal-table workload showed a large difference too.

I am quite happy to accept arguments in favour of Go, but a hundredfold difference on such an ordinary workload is worth examining before declaring one language a hundred times better than another, because V8 is an enormously sophisticated piece of engineering. When we looked, much of the cost wasn't JavaScript at all; it was the execution model. In the existing transpiler output, ABAP values are runtime objects, arithmetic goes through the runtime's operations, and every method call is asynchronous, with async and await throughout the generated code. These are sensible choices for a general runtime that must emulate ABAP, but in a recursive workload each tiny call carries that machinery with it.

Our new IR had already worked out the types, conversions and operations, so we tried emitting JavaScript from the same IR, with plain values where the semantics allow it and synchronous calls. And here is the part I particularly enjoyed: the new JavaScript was dramatically faster too. Fibonacci went from about 24 ms in the transpiled JavaScript to 0.96 ms in JavaScript generated from the IR, and to 0.24 ms in Go, so Go was still ahead, but by about four times rather than a hundred; the million-row table went from 311 ms to 11.3 ms, against 8.7 ms in Go. Across the measured workloads, the new JavaScript path was roughly 7–28 times faster than the original transpiler output.

We set out to make ABAP faster with Go, and found how to make it much faster in JavaScript first. The same typed IR emitted as JavaScript, with plain values and synchronous calls, takes Fibonacci(25) from 24 ms to under 1 ms; Go adds the last step. One machine, two programs, not a ranking of languages.

Source: tools/gogen/README.md, “Language or model? The same IR emitted as JS” (measured 2026-09-23; 16-core x86-64 WSL2, Node 26.9, Go 1.26.0). The README has two more workloads (primes, a table of 10⁶ rows) with the same pattern.

These are measurements of particular programs and runtime versions, not a universal language ranking, and the gogen research notes contain the workloads, the environment and the numbers. What interested me was the explanation: the biggest improvement came from moving decisions into the compiler, instead of making the runtime work them out again and again.

Because the same IR can be emitted as both Go and JavaScript, we now also had two implementations to compare with each other and with SAP. Agreement between two backends is useful evidence, but the original ABAP behaviour remains the reference, since independent implementations can make independent mistakes.

There was one more twist: we compiled the Go to WebAssembly and ran it in a browser, and for the measured rendering workloads the IR-generated JavaScript was faster than Go/WASM, partly because the latter carries a larger runtime and different execution costs. So after setting out to make everything better with Go, we had made JavaScript better as well. I consider this an excellent outcome. 😃

And then the whole server wanted to leave

By this point, turning one ABAP report into a native program worked. But Open SteamGate already contained a substantial collection of ABAP classes, including its Gateway and the services behind the demo applications, so the next question was whether we could compile those too.

That is how OSGo happened. Instead of building one report with a small runtime closure, OSGo compiles the supported part of Open SteamGate's application-server runtime to Go: one native executable with the compiled ABAP services and their initial data, and SQLite through a Go driver. Start the binary, and it serves actual OData requests, with no JavaScript server process and no separate database server in that configuration. It doesn't yet provide every feature of the Node-based OSG host — in particular, it doesn't serve the ADT façade — but running the OData side as one executable was already a substantial milestone.

OSGo: the whole server as one Go binary.
 
A real OData request and its JSON answer.

There is something pleasing about compiling an application-server implementation written in ABAP into a Go executable and then using that executable to serve ABAP applications. It is a little recursive, but we seem to be getting used to that.

The report compiler gives us another practical possibility: ABAP programs that are useful without behaving like application servers at all. A report that transforms files, analyses data or runs a batch operation can become a native command with its own SQLite database, taking its arguments from a script or asking for them in the terminal, and the ABAP doesn't have to be rewritten just because its destination has changed. Once the compiler knows enough about a program, the place where it runs becomes a design choice rather than an assumption built into the language.

Of course, someone may reasonably ask whether this means my ABAP can run on a ZX Spectrum as well.

 
ZX Spectrum: FLEET.bin · ABAP → MinZ HIR → MIR2 → Z80 · sha256 2d52a6a2…dc74 · real capture, 10 s of emulated time, original 352×304 frames, no crop, scaling or compositing; not a benchmark. MZX emulator, Pentagon 128 model; the TR-DOS disk image is read through sector traps, no system or DOS ROM executed; no physical-hardware claim. The same 1,875-byte ABAP source as below. minz PR #203, merged.
 
 
CP/M: FLEET.COM · ABAP → MinZ HIR → MIR2 → Z80 · real capture, unmodified frames, about 8 s; Z80/MZE CP/M emulation, no physical-hardware claim. The same 1,875-byte ABAP report: F4 → FLEET.CSV → GUI_UPLOAD → typed table → cl_salv_table.
 
Agon: FLEET.BIN · ABAP → MinZ HIR → MIR2 → Z80-mode code on eZ80 · real capture, unmodified frames, real debugger pauses, not a benchmark. Both MinZ PRs are merged (#200, #201).

AgonLight2 (powered by eZ80) is quite a remarkable computer, by the way: AgonLight2 - Open Source Hardware Board

It can, a little. That is a different compiler, MinZ, with a rather smaller processor and its own adventures, including the occasional emulator that starts quite happily and then declines to execute the program we gave it. We'll get back to that one; I still have a terminal to show you.

Try letting your ABAP out

If you want to play with this, start with the examples under gogen in Open SteamGate. Building the native executables needs the development toolchain, including Go 1.26, but the resulting binaries can be copied and run on their target platform on their own. In a checkout, osd run compiles and runs a report in one step, and F8 on a report in VS Code does the same.

For an application-sized example, osg-demo has a chapter called My ABAP Escaped from the Server, which follows an airship-fleet report as its selection screen becomes a terminal form, its parameters become command-line options, and its local tables become a SQLite database. The fleet has been remarkably patient with this project, and I am beginning to suspect that the Old Boiler is less an airship and more an integration-test platform.

And I particularly recommend the file-selection example, zpickfile, because pressing F4 on a native command-line program generated from ABAP is something I still find entertaining.

And one more: F4 picks a CSV, cl_gui_frontend_services=>gui_upload reads it, and the report lists it with the headings from its first line.

BTW, does it look like R/2?

If you manage to break it, I'd genuinely like to know how. There are plenty of ABAP constructs and runtime behaviours still to implement, and a small report that behaves differently on SAP and on the native runtime is exactly what helps an independent implementation improve.

I started by wanting to run ABAP outside SAP, then without a server, and then I wanted the report's selection screen back. Along the way we ended up with a typed representation of ABAP, two code-generation backends, a faster JavaScript path and a Go application-server runtime — quite a journey for a report that only wanted to print a few lines. I still like JavaScript, I still like Go, and I now have ABAP programs that can travel between them, which is quite a nice place to be.

Except that, somewhere around the same time, I started working on another question. If we can compile ABAP into JavaScript and Go, what happens if we turn the whole arrangement around, take code written in TypeScript, and compile it into ABAP? And perhaps take an entire tool such as abaplint, written in TypeScript, and run it inside the very ABAP system whose code it was created to inspect?

It was not the first idea. Lars and I had been circling this question for a while, independently and not quite independently, each borrowing the other’s successes and failures in roughly equal measure. Lars went first with abap-wasm, a WebAssembly virtual machine written in ABAP: nearly everything compiles to WASM these days, so an interpreter for it on the stack opens a large door at once. I had spent some time on interpreters of my own by then — zork-abap runs Infocom’s Z-machine on SAP, cpm-abap is a Z80/i8080 emulator that runs CP/M programs, and there was a 6502 as well — so I thought a WASM compiler, rather than an interpreter, might be the more promising route. It turned out that WASM sits at too low a level of abstraction for the lift back to ABAP: you get a stack machine and a linear memory, and everything that would make the output readable has already been compiled away.

interpreting twice is interpreting too often - the fifth approach moves the work into a compiler

So I tried from the other end, with a JavaScript interpreter, which became ZMJS, a mini JavaScript engine in about two thousand lines of ABAP. It runs on a real system and even runs the abaplint lexer there. Lars then did the serious version, ZQJS, a port of Fabrice Bellard’s QuickJS engine to ABAP, which is a far more complete JavaScript. Both work. Both were too slow for the practical target, which was running abaplint itself on the stack, in a time a developer would wait for; an interpreter written in an interpreted language is interpreting twice, and that is at least once too often.

What I had left was the MinZ frontend. MinZ already lowers several languages — Nanz, MinZ, Lizp, Lanz, ABAP, PL/M, Pascal — into one high-level intermediate representation, HIR, before any of them goes anywhere near a Z80. So what if TypeScript and JavaScript were lowered into that same HIR, and then lifted back out as idiomatic ABAP? Classes, functions, closures and interfaces look remarkably alike across modern languages; the real differences are small and nameable, the main one being that JavaScript treats arrays as references while ABAP treats internal tables as values. Differences of that kind can be handled as explicit edge cases, and the rewrites that handle them are stated once in Grace, an S-expression language for rewriting and optimisation, rather than scattered through a code generator. That is ABAPiti, and it is where abaplint, written in TypeScript, comes back to the stack as ABAP.

Well. It seems ABAP was leaving the application server just as TypeScript was arriving.

They must have passed each other on the way. 😃

Next time: ABAPiti — A Journey Towards Self-Hosting.

Open SteamGate · gogen / osabap / OSGo · osg-demo · ABAPiti

P.S. I Ported SAP* to a 1976 CPU. It Wasn't That Slow. | LinkedIn - now it is true* =)))

entry.title: Building a RAP Managed Business Object on SAP BTP — A Complete Step-by-Step Guide
entry.content:
SAP RAP Managed Scenario — Step-by-Step Guide

                         A complete, beginner-friendly implementation of an SAP ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model (RAP) Managed Business Object — built on SAP BTP ABAP Environment Trial. This repository walks through every layer of the RAP stack from database tables to the Fiori Elements UI, with detailed explanations of why each artifact exists, not just how to create it.

Table of Contents

  • Overview
  • Architecture
  • Prerequisites
  • Step 1 — Database Table
  • Step 2 — Draft Table
  • Step 3 — Interface View (Z*_I)
  • Step 4 — Consumption View (Z*_C)
  • Step 5 — Metadata Extension
  • Step 6 — Behavior Definition (Interface)
  • Step 7 — Behavior Definition (Projection)
  • Step 8 — Behavior Implementation
  • Step 9 — Service Definition & Binding
  • Key Takeaways

 

Overview
What is RAP?
                         The ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model (RAP) is SAP's modern, cloud-ready framework for building transactional Fiori applications in ABAP Cloud. It replaces older approaches like BOPF and classic ABAP MVC, and is the standard for SAP S/4HANA Cloud and BTP ABAP Environment development.
 
RAP provides:
  • A structured, layered architecture from database to UI
  • Built-in OData service generation (no manual SEGW needed)
  • Framework-managed CRUD operations (Create, Read, Update, Delete)
  • Draft handling for save/resume workflows
  • Clean Core compliance — no modifications to SAP standard objects

What is the Managed Scenario?

TypeWho handles CRUD?When to use
ManagedRAP Framework automaticallyNew custom BOs — no legacy dependencies
UnmanagedDeveloper writes all logicWrapping legacy function modules / BAPIs

In the Managed scenario, the RAP framework automatically handles database INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, and SELECT operations. You only write code for custom business logic like validations, determinations, and custom actions. This makes it the fastest and cleanest way to build a new Business Object from scratch.

 

  Architecture

The RAP stack follows a strict layered architecture. Each layer has a specific responsibility, and no layer should skip or bypass another.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                                            Fiori Elements UI                                                                    │
│                                                                   (Auto-generated from OData)                                                      │
└────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────┘
                                                                             │ OData V4
┌────────────────────────▼────────────────────────────────┐
│                                           Service Definition + Service Binding                                                                   │
│                                       (Exposes which entities go into OData)                                                                 │
└────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────┘
                                                                             │
┌────────────────────────▼────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                          PROJECTION LAYER (ZC_*)                                                                   │
│                                    CDS Consumption View + Projection Behavior Def.                                              │
│                                   (Service-specific: UI annotations, field exposure)                                                  │
└────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────┘
                                                                             │ as projection on
┌────────────────────────▼────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                   INTERFACE LAYER (ZR_* / ZI_*)                                                                   │
│                                       CDS Interface View + Base Behavior Definition                                                   │
│                                        (Service-agnostic: data model, business logic)                                                  │
└────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────┘
                                                                              │
┌────────────────────────▼────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                                 DATABASE LAYER                                                                               │
│                                                    Main Table (ZDB_*) + Draft Table (*_D)                                                     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Prerequisites

Before you start, make sure you have:

  • SAP BTP Trial account — 
  • Steps to create Trial account 
  • ABAP Environment trial instance provisioned on BTP 
  • Eclipse IDE with ABAP Development Tools (ADT) plugin installed 
  • Connected to your BTP ABAP system via ADT
  • Basic understanding of ABAP syntax and CDS views

Step 1 — Database Table (Main Table)

What is it?

The database table is the foundation of your Business Object. It is the actual physical table in the SAP HANA database where all your application data is permanently stored. Every field you want to persist — travel ID, agency, customer, price, status — must be defined here first.

Why do we create it?

Without a database table, there is no place to store data. The entire RAP stack above it — CDS views, behavior definitions, OData services — are all abstractions built on top of this table. The table is the single source of truth for your BO's data.

Structure of a RAP-compliant database table

A RAP managed table must follow specific conventions:

@EndUserText.label : 'Products'
@AbapCatalog.enhancement.category : #NOT_EXTENSIBLE
@AbapCatalog.tableCategory : #TRANSPARENT
@AbapCatalog.deliveryClass : #A
@AbapCatalog.dataMaintenance : #RESTRICTED
define table znk_t_product {

  key client            : abap.clnt not null;
  key pro_uuid          : sysuuid_x16 not null;
  key product_id        : abap.char(10) not null;
  description           : abap.char(40);
  @Semantics.quantity.unitOfMeasure : 'znk_t_product.uom'
  qty                   : abap.quan(8,3);
  uom                   : abap.unit(3);
  @Semantics.amount.currencyCode : 'znk_t_product.currency'
  price                 : abap.curr(15,2);
  currency              : abap.cuky;
  mfg_date              : abap.datn;
  exp_date              : abap.datn;
  validdays             : abap.int4;
  plant                 : abap.char(4);
  local_created_by      : abp_creation_user;
  local_created_at      : abp_creation_tstmpl;
  local_last_changed_by : abp_locinst_lastchange_user;
  local_last_changed_at : abp_locinst_lastchange_tstmpl;
  last_changed_at       : abp_lastchange_tstmpl;

}

Important: The last_changed_at field with type abp_lastchange_tstmpl is critical for the ETag mechanism. When two users try to update the same record simultaneously, RAP compares this timestamp to detect conflicts and reject stale updates.

Key fields explained

FieldTypePurpose

clientabap.clntSAP client field — mandatory first key in every table
product_idBusiness keyUnique identifier for each product record
local_created_byy / local_created_atAdmin fieldsAuto-populated by RAP framework — track who created the record
local_last_changed_by / local_last_changed_atAdmin fieldsAuto-populated — track last modifier
last_changed_atETag fieldUsed by RAP for optimistic locking / concurrency control

 

Step 2 — Draft Table (Why It Exists)

What is a Draft Table?

The draft table is a temporary storage table where incomplete, unsaved data is held while a user is still filling in a form. It has an identical structure to your main database table, with some additional draft-specific fields added by the framework.

By convention, draft tables are named the same as the main table with a _D suffix:

Main table   : ZNK_T_PRODUCT        ← permanent, saved data
Draft table  : ZNK_T_PRODUCT_D      ← temporary, in-progress data
 

Why do we need a Draft Table?

Imagine a user opens a "Create Product" form in a Fiori app and starts filling in the fields — Plant, UOM, MFG & Exp dates. Halfway through, their browser crashes, or they need to attend a meeting. Without draft handling, all their work is lost.

With Draft Handling:

User opens form
      │
      ▼
Data saved to DRAFT TABLE immediately (auto-save)
      │
      ├── User continues tomorrow → draft is still there ✅
      ├── User switches device → draft is still there ✅
      └── User clicks "Save" → data moves to MAIN TABLE ✅
                               draft record is deleted ✅
 

The draft table ensures no data loss during long-running create/edit operations. It also enables the "Edit" button behavior in Fiori apps — when you click Edit on a saved record, RAP copies the record to the draft table so your edits don't affect the live data until you explicitly save.

How to define the Draft Table

You don't write the draft table manually field by field. You reference it in your Behavior Definition and let ADT generate it:

-- In your Behavior Definition:
managed implementation in class zbp_nk_product_i unique;
strict ( 2 );
with draft;
define behavior for znk_product_I //alias <alias_name>
persistent table znk_t_product               -- ← your main table
draft table znk_t_product_d                  -- ← your draft table (RAP manages this)            
...
 

When you activate the behavior definition, ADT automatically creates the draft table with the correct structure.

Draft Table vs Main Table — Side by Side

AspectMain TableDraft Table
PurposePermanent business dataTemporary in-progress data
When data lands hereOn "Save" actionOn every field change (auto-save)
Who can see itAll usersOnly the user editing
Deleted whenNever (business record)On Save or Discard
NamedZNK_T_PRODUCTZNK_T_PRODUCT_D
Created byDeveloper manuallyADT generates from BDEF
 
 
     Step 3 — Interface View (Z*_I)

What is the Interface View?

The Interface View is the base CDS View Entity that sits directly on top of your database table. It forms the service-agnostic data model of your Business Object — meaning it defines the complete data structure without any UI-specific concerns.

By convention, Interface Views are prefixed with ZR_ (R = Root) for root entities or ZI_ (I = Interface).

@AccessControl.authorizationCheck: #NOT_REQUIRED
@EndUserText.label: 'Product Interface View'
@Metadata.ignorePropagatedAnnotations: true
define root view entity znk_product_I as select from znk_t_product
association [0..1] to I_Currency as _Currency on $projection.Currency = _Currency.Currency
association [ 0..1] to I_UnitOfMeasure as _Uom on $projection.Uom = _Uom.UnitOfMeasure

{
    key pro_uuid as ProUuid,
    key product_id as ProductId,
    description as Description,
    @Semantics.quantity.unitOfMeasure: 'uom'
    qty as Qty,
    @Consumption.valueHelpDefinition: [{ 
    entity.name: 'I_UnitOfMeasure',
    entity.element: 'UnitOfMeasure',
    useForValidation: true
     }]
    uom as Uom,
    @Semantics.amount.currencyCode: 'currency'
    price as Price,
    @Consumption.valueHelpDefinition: [{ 
    entity.name: 'I_Currency',
    entity.element: 'Currency',
    useForValidation: true
     }]
    currency as Currency,
    mfg_date as MfgDate,
    exp_date as ExpDate,
    plant as Plant,
    validdays as ValidDays,
    @Semantics.user.createdBy: true
    local_created_by as LocalCreatedBy,
    @Semantics.systemDateTime.createdAt: true
    local_created_at as LocalCreatedAt,
    @Semantics.user.lastChangedBy: true
    local_last_changed_by as LocalLastChangedBy,
    @Semantics.systemDateTime.localInstanceLastChangedAt: true
    local_last_changed_at as LocalLastChangedAt,
    @Semantics.systemDateTime.lastChangedAt: true
    last_changed_at as LastChangedAt,
    _Uom as UomDetails,
    _Currency as CurrencyDetails
     // Make association public
}

Why do we need the Interface View?

The Interface View serves several critical purposes:

1. Abstraction from the database table The database table uses technical field names and types. The Interface View can rename, cast, and join fields into a cleaner business model. If the table structure changes, only the interface view needs to be updated — everything above is unaffected.

2. It is the root of the composition tree The keyword define root view entity declares this as the top of a Business Object hierarchy. All child entities (like Booking under Travel) are connected back to this root via COMPOSITION OF associations.

3. It is reusable across multiple services The interface view has NO UI annotations, NO Fiori-specific logic. This means the same interface view can power:

  • A Fiori Elements app (via projection view → OData)
  • A remote API (via a different projection)

4. Associations are defined here Associations to related entities (Currency, UnitOfMeasure) are defined on the interface view so they are available to all Products.

The define root view entity keyword

This keyword does two important things:

  • It declares this CDS view as a Root Entity of a Business Object
  • It enables it to have its own Behavior Definition repository object
  • Only root entities can define composition of child associations
  Step 4 — Consumption View (Z*_C)

What is the Consumption View?

The Consumption View (also called the Projection View) sits on top of the Interface View and represents a service-specific, tailored window into the Business Object. It is what gets exposed to the outside world — via OData, via a Fiori app, via an API.

By convention, Consumption Views are prefixed or suffixed with ZC_ (C = Consumption).

@AccessControl.authorizationCheck: #NOT_REQUIRED
@EndUserText.label: 'Product Consumption View'
@Metadata.ignorePropagatedAnnotations: true
@Metadata.allowExtensions: true
define root view entity znk_product_c
  provider contract transactional_query as projection on znk_product_I                           -- ← the key syntax: "as projection on"
  association [1..1] to znk_product_I as _BaseEntity on $projection.ProUuid = _BaseEntity.ProUuid
                                                    and $projection.ProductId = _BaseEntity.ProductId
{
key ProUuid,
key ProductId,
Description,
@Semantics.quantity.unitOfMeasure: 'Uom'
Qty,
@Consumption.valueHelpDefinition:[{ entity:{ name: 'I_UnitOfMeasure',
                                             element: 'UnitOfMeasure'},
                                    useForValidation: true }]
Uom,
@Semantics.amount.currencyCode: 'Currency'
Price,
@Consumption.valueHelpDefinition: [{ entity:{ name: 'I_Currency',
                                     element: 'Currency' },
                                     useForValidation: true  }]
Currency,
MfgDate,
ExpDate,
Plant,
ValidDays,
LocalCreatedBy,
LocalCreatedAt,
LocalLastChangedBy,
LocalLastChangedAt,
LastChangedAt,
/* Associations */
UomDetails,
CurrencyDetails,
_BaseEntity
}
 

Why do we need the Consumption View if we already have the Interface View?

This is the most common question from beginners. The answer is separation of concerns:

 
Concern Interface View✅Consumption View
Business data model✅Defined hereInherited from interface
Associations & compositions✅Defined hereRedirected here
UI annotations (@UI.*)❌Not here✅Via Metadata Extension
Value helps (@Consumption.valueHelpDefinition)❌Not here✅Defined here
Field aliasing for UI❌Not here✅Can rename fields
Access control✅Defined hereAdditional checks possible
Which fields to exposeAll fieldsSubset — only what the app needs

Real-world analogy:             

                       Think of the Interface View as a master employee record with every piece of data. The Consumption View is a role-specific form an HR manager sees salary and personal data, a project manager sees only skills and availability. Same underlying data, different projections.

The as projection on syntax

This is what makes a view a projection view. It tells the RAP framework:

  • "This view is consuming/projecting another view"
  • "The underlying BO's behavior definition applies through here"
  • "Compositions must be redirected to their own projection equivalents"

🎨Step 5 — Metadata Extension

What is a Metadata Extension?

A Metadata Extension (.ddlx file) is a separate repository object that holds UI annotations for a CDS view, kept completely separate from the view's data model definition. It is applied on top of a Consumption View that has @Metadata.allowExtensions: true.

@Metadata.layer: #CORE
@UI.headerInfo: { typeName: 'Product', typeNamePlural: 'Products' }
annotate entity znk_product_c with
{

@UI.facet: [{ id: 'Info',
              type: #IDENTIFICATION_REFERENCE,
              label: 'Product',
              position: 10}]
  @UI:{ lineItem: [{position: 10, label: 'Product ID', importance: #HIGH,hidden: true},
                   { type: #FOR_ACTION, dataAction: 'checkProductValidity', label: 'Check Validity', position: 10 ,emphasized: true},              --- Custom Button Added Here 
                   { type: #FOR_ACTION, dataAction: 'clearValidDays',       label: 'Clear',          position: 20 ,emphasized: true}],             --- Custom Button Added Here   
        identification: [{position: 10, label: 'Product ID', importance: #HIGH, hidden: true},
                         { type: #FOR_ACTION, dataAction: 'checkProductValidity', label: 'Check Validity', position: 10 }] }
  ProUuid;
  @UI:{ lineItem: [{position: 20, label: 'Product ID', importance: #HIGH}],
        identification: [{position: 20, label: 'Product ID', importance: #HIGH}],
        selectionField: [{ position: 10  }] }
  ProductId;
  @UI:{ lineItem: [{position: 30, label: 'Description', importance: #HIGH}],
        identification: [{position: 30, label: 'Description', importance: #HIGH}],
        selectionField: [{ position: 30  }] }
  Description;
   @UI:{ lineItem: [{position: 31, label: 'Qty', importance: #HIGH}],
        identification: [{position: 31, label: 'Quantity', importance: #HIGH}] }
  Qty;
  @UI:{ lineItem: [{position: 40, label: 'UOM', importance: #HIGH, hidden: true}],
        identification: [{position: 40, label: 'Unit Of Measurement', importance: #HIGH, hidden: true}] }
  Uom;
  @UI:{ lineItem: [{position: 50, label: 'Price', importance: #HIGH}],
        identification: [{position: 50, label: 'Price', importance: #HIGH}] }
  Price;
  @UI:{ lineItem: [{position: 60, label: 'Currency', importance: #HIGH,hidden: true}],
        identification: [{position: 60, label: 'Currency', importance: #HIGH, hidden: true}] }
  Currency;
  @UI:{ lineItem: [{position: 70, label: 'MFG Date', importance: #HIGH, hidden: true}],
        identification: [{position: 70, label: 'Manufacture Date', importance: #HIGH}] }
  MfgDate;
  @UI:{ lineItem: [{position: 80, label: 'Exp. Date', importance: #HIGH, hidden: true}],
        identification: [{position: 80, label: 'Expiry Date', importance: #HIGH}] }
  ExpDate;
  @UI:{ lineItem: [{position: 90, label: 'Plant', importance: #HIGH}],
        identification: [{position: 90, label: 'Plant', importance: #HIGH}] }
  Plant;
   @UI:{ lineItem: [{position: 91, label: 'Valid Days', importance: #HIGH}],
        identification: [{position: 91, label: 'Valid Days', importance: #HIGH}],
        selectionField: [{ position: 91  }] }
  ValidDays;
  @UI:{ lineItem: [{position: 100, label: 'Created By', importance: #HIGH}],
        identification: [{position: 100, label: 'Created By', importance: #HIGH}] }
  LocalCreatedBy;
  @UI:{ lineItem: [{position: 110, label: 'Created At', importance: #HIGH }],
        identification: [{position: 110, label: 'Created At', importance: #HIGH}] }
  LocalCreatedAt;
  @UI:{ lineItem: [{position: 120, label: 'Last Changed By', importance: #HIGH, hidden: true }],
        identification: [{position: 120, label: 'Last Changed By', importance: #HIGH}] }
  LocalLastChangedBy;
  @UI:{ lineItem: [{position: 130, label: 'Last Changed At', importance: #HIGH, hidden: true}],
        identification: [{position: 130, label: 'Last Changed At', importance: #HIGH}] }
  LocalLastChangedAt;
  @UI:{ lineItem: [{position: 140, label: 'Last Changed At', importance: #HIGH, hidden: true}],
        identification: [{position: 140, label: 'Product ID', importance: #HIGH, hidden: true}] }
  LastChangedAt;

}
 

Why do we use a Metadata Extension instead of putting annotations directly in the CDS view?

There are three powerful reasons:

1. Clean Separation of Concerns The CDS view defines WHAT data exists. The Metadata Extension defines HOW it looks in the UI. Mixing both in one file creates a massive, hard-to-read view definition. Separating them keeps each file focused and maintainable.

2. Extensibility (Key User / Partner / Customer layers) The @Metadata.layer annotation supports a hierarchy:

#CORE          ← SAP / developer defines base UI
#CUSTOMER      ← Customer adds their annotations
#PARTNER       ← Relates to a partner extension of a product 
#INDUSTRY      ← Relates to an industry-specific extension of a product (SAP Industry Solution)
 

Lower layers can be overridden by higher layers without modifying the original files. This is the foundation of SAP's extensibility model.

3. Keeps the CDS View Clean for Multiple Consumers If you put @UI.lineItem directly in the CDS view, those annotations are baked in for everyone. With a metadata extension, different services can have different metadata extensions on the same projection view — different UI layouts for different apps.

Common UI Annotations in Metadata Extensions

 
AnnotationPurposeExample
@UI.lineItemShow field in the list tableList page columns
@UI.identificationShow field in the detail formObject page fields
@UI.selectionFieldShow field in the filter barSearch filters
@UI.facetDefine sections/tabs on the object page"Product Details" tab
@UI.hiddenHide field from UI entirelyInternal fields
@UI.dataActionAdd a button for a custom action"Valid Days" button

⚙️Step 6 — Behavior Definition (Interface View)

What is a Behavior Definition?

A Behavior Definition (BDEF) is a repository object that defines what operations are allowed on a Business Object. It answers questions like:

  • Can this BO be created, updated, deleted?
  • Which fields are read-only or mandatory?
  • Does it support draft handling?
  • What custom actions exist (like "Valid Days")?
  • How are primary keys generated?

Interface View Behavior Definition

The base BDEF sits on the Interface View and defines the complete set of capabilities of the BO:

managed implementation in class zbp_nk_product_i unique;
strict ( 2 );
with draft;
define behavior for znk_product_I //alias <alias_name>
persistent table znk_t_product
draft table znk_t_product_d
lock master                                                         -- Locking mechanism
total etag LastChangedAt
authorization master ( global )
etag master LastChangedAt                                           -- ETag for concurrency control
{

 -- Field controls
 field ( mandatory : create ) ProductId;                            -- Makes Mandatory when create
 field ( readonly )                                                 -- Makes non-editable
 LocalCreatedAt,
 LocalCreatedBy,
 LocalLastChangedAt,
 LocalLastChangedBy,
 LastChangedAt;
 field ( numbering : managed ) ProUuid;                             -- Makes Numbering Managed
 field ( readonly : update ) ProUuid, ProductId;                    -- Makes non-editable when update

   -- Standard CRUD operations (framework handles automatically in managed)
  create;
  update;
  delete;

  -- Custom actions (developer implements)
  action  ( features : instance ) checkProductValidity result [1] $self;
  action  ( features : instance ) clearValidDays result [1] $self;

  -- Draft related Actions
  draft action Edit;
  draft action Activate optimized;
  draft action Discard;
  draft action Resume;
  draft determine action Prepare;

  -- Mapping is very important to store the values to DB 
  mapping for znk_t_product
    {
      ProUuid            = pro_uuid;
      ProductId          = product_id;
      Description        = description;
      Qty                = qty;
      Uom                = uom;
      Price              = price;
      Currency           = currency;
      MfgDate            = mfg_date;
      ExpDate            = exp_date;
      Plant              = plant;
      ValidDays          = validdays;
      LocalCreatedBy     = local_created_by;
      LocalCreatedAt     = local_created_at;
      LocalLastChangedAt = local_last_changed_at;
      LocalLastChangedBy = local_last_changed_by;
      LastChangedAt      = last_changed_at;
    }
}
 

Key BDEF keywords explained

managed — Tells the RAP framework to auto-handle all database operations (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE). You don't write any MODIFY dbtab statements yourself.

with draft — Activates the draft handling mechanism. The framework will use your draft table for all in-progress changes.

etag master LocalLastChangedAt — Enables optimistic locking. Before any update, RAP compares the LocalLastChangedAt timestamp in the request with the database to detect if someone else modified the record in between.

lock master — When a user starts editing (enters draft mode), the record is locked so no other user can simultaneously edit the same record.

numbering:managed — (when used on a field) Tells the framework to auto-generate a UUID primary key at CREATE time — no manual key assignment needed.

validation — A method you implement in the Behavior Implementation class. Called by the framework before save. Return error messages to block the save.

determination — A method that auto-runs when specific fields change. Used for defaulting values (e.g., set status to "Open" when a Product is created).

action — A custom operation beyond standard CRUD. Adds a button in the Fiori UI. Example: "Valid Days" changes status to Accepted.

🔒Step 7 — Behavior Definition (Projection View)

What is the Projection Behavior Definition?

The Projection BDEF sits on the Consumption View and exposes a subset of the base BDEF's operations for a specific service. It acts as a gatekeeper — you decide which operations this particular OData service gets to offer.

projection;
strict ( 2 );
use draft;

define behavior for znk_product_c //alias <alias_name>
{
  use create;                           -- Expose create to this service
  use update;                           -- Expose update to this service
  use delete;                           -- Expose delete to this service

  use action Edit;
  use action Activate;
  use action Discard;
  use action Prepare;
  use action Resume;


  -- Expose only the custom actions this service needs
  use action checkProductValidity;
  use action clearValidDays;
}
 

Interface BDEF vs Projection BDEF — Why both?

    
 Interface BDEFProjection BDEF
Sits onInterface View (Z*_R)Consumption View (Z*_C)
ContainsALL possible operationsSUBSET for this service
ImplementationDeveloper writes code hereJust use statements — no code
ReusabilityOne per BOOne per service/app
AnalogyFull employee recordRole-specific access form

Imagine you have two apps using the same Travel BO:

  • Admin App → projection BDEF exposes: create, update, delete, ValidDays, Clear
  • Read-Only Report App → projection BDEF exposes: nothing (read-only by omission)

Same base BO, completely different service behavior — controlled purely by the projection BDEF.

💻Step 8 — Behavior Implementation (BAP)

What is the Behavior Implementation?

The Behavior Implementation is an ABAP class that contains the actual code for all custom operations defined in the base Behavior Definition — validations, determinations, and actions. In managed scenarios, you do NOT write code for standard CRUD — the framework handles that. You only write code for your custom business logic.

The class is named in the BDEF with implementation in class zbp_nk_product_i unique;.

"! <p class="shorttext synchronized" lang="en">Behavior Implementation for ZNK_PRODUCT_I</p>
CLASS zbp_nk_product_i DEFINITION PUBLIC ABSTRACT FINAL FOR BEHAVIOR OF znk_product_i.
ENDCLASS.

CLASS zbp_nk_product_i IMPLEMENTATION.
ENDCLASS.
 

The actual logic sits in local classes inside the implementation class's .locals_imp include:

Validation Example — validateDates

CLASS lhc_znk_product_I DEFINITION INHERITING FROM cl_abap_behavior_handler.
  PRIVATE SECTION.
    METHODS get_global_authorizations FOR GLOBAL AUTHORIZATION
    REQUEST requested_authorizations FOR znk_product_I RESULT result.
    METHODS checkProductValidity FOR MODIFY
       keys FOR ACTION znk_product_I~checkProductValidity RESULT result.
    METHODS get_instance_features FOR INSTANCE FEATURES
      keys REQUEST requested_features FOR znk_product_I RESULT result.
    METHODS clearvaliddays FOR MODIFY
       keys FOR ACTION znk_product_i~clearvaliddays RESULT result.
ENDCLASS.

CLASS lhc_znk_product_I IMPLEMENTATION.
  METHOD get_global_authorizations.
  ENDMETHOD.

  METHOD checkProductValidity.

    READ ENTITIES OF znk_product_I IN LOCAL MODE                               --Read entries from Interface view to lt_products
        ENTITY znk_product_I
        FIELDS ( MfgDate ExpDate )
        WITH CORRESPONDING #( keys )
        RESULT DATA(lt_products)
        FAILED DATA(ls_failed).

    MODIFY ENTITIES OF znk_product_I IN LOCAL MODE                             --Modify entries from Interface view to lt_products
        ENTITY znk_product_I
        UPDATE FIELDS ( ValidDays )
        WITH VALUE #(
          FOR ls IN lt_products
          LET lv_days = CONV i( ls-ExpDate - ls-MfgDate )
          IN ( %tky      = ls-%tky
               ValidDays = lv_days ) ).

    LOOP AT lt_products INTO DATA(ls_product).                                  --Validation on to lt_products
      IF ls_product-ExpDate <= ls_product-MfgDate.
        APPEND VALUE #(
          %tky = ls_product-%tky
          %msg = new_message_with_text(
                   severity = if_abap_behv_message=>severity-error
                   text     = 'Expiry Date must be after Manufacturing Date!' )
        ) TO reported-znk_product_i.
      ENDIF.
    ENDLOOP.
    READ ENTITIES OF znk_product_I IN LOCAL MODE
                                   ENTITY znk_product_I
                                   ALL FIELDS
                                   WITH CORRESPONDING #( keys )
                                   RESULT DATA(lt_result).

    result = VALUE #( FOR ls IN lt_result                                        --Return the modified entries to result
                      ( %tky   = ls-%tky
                        %param = ls ) ).   

  ENDMETHOD.

  METHOD get_instance_features.
    READ ENTITIES OF znk_product_I IN LOCAL MODE
     ENTITY znk_product_I
     FIELDS ( ProductId )
     WITH CORRESPONDING #( keys )
     RESULT DATA(lt_products)
     FAILED DATA(ls_failed).

    result = VALUE #( FOR ls IN lt_products
                      ( %tky                          = ls-%tky
                        %action-checkProductValidity  = if_abap_behv=>fc-o-enabled ) ).
  ENDMETHOD.

  METHOD clearValidDays.
    READ ENTITIES OF znk_product_I IN LOCAL MODE
        ENTITY znk_product_I
        FIELDS ( MfgDate ExpDate )
        WITH CORRESPONDING #( keys )
        RESULT DATA(lt_products)
        FAILED DATA(ls_failed).

    MODIFY ENTITIES OF znk_product_I IN LOCAL MODE
        ENTITY znk_product_I
        UPDATE FIELDS ( ValidDays )
        WITH VALUE #(
          FOR ls IN lt_products
          LET lv_days = 0
          IN ( %tky      = ls-%tky
               ValidDays = lv_days ) ).

    READ ENTITIES OF znk_product_I IN LOCAL MODE
                      ENTITY znk_product_I
                      ALL FIELDS
                      WITH CORRESPONDING #( keys )
                      RESULT DATA(lt_result).
    result = VALUE #( FOR ls IN lt_result
        ( %tky   = ls-%tky
          %param = ls ) ).   
  ENDMETHOD.

ENDCLASS.
 

Determination Example — setInitialStatus

METHOD setInitialStatus.
  " Read travels that were just created
  READ ENTITIES OF zr_traveltp IN LOCAL MODE
    ENTITY Travel
      FIELDS ( OverallStatus )
      WITH CORRESPONDING #( keys )
    RESULT DATA(lt_travel)
    FAILED failed.

  " Filter: only set status if it's initial (empty)
  DELETE lt_travel WHERE OverallStatus IS NOT INITIAL.
  CHECK lt_travel IS NOT INITIAL.

  " Set default status to 'Open'
  MODIFY ENTITIES OF zr_traveltp IN LOCAL MODE
    ENTITY Travel
      UPDATE FIELDS ( OverallStatus )
      WITH VALUE #( FOR ls_travel IN lt_travel (
        %tky          = ls_travel-%tky
        OverallStatus = 'O'   " O = Open
      ) )
    REPORTED DATA(lt_reported).

  reported = CORRESPONDING #( DEEP lt_reported ).
ENDMETHOD.
 

Action Example — checkProductValidity

METHOD checkProductValidity.

    READ ENTITIES OF znk_product_I IN LOCAL MODE
        ENTITY znk_product_I
        FIELDS ( MfgDate ExpDate )
        WITH CORRESPONDING #( keys )
        RESULT DATA(lt_products)
        FAILED DATA(ls_failed).

    MODIFY ENTITIES OF znk_product_I IN LOCAL MODE
        ENTITY znk_product_I
        UPDATE FIELDS ( ValidDays )
        WITH VALUE #(
          FOR ls IN lt_products
          LET lv_days = CONV i( ls-ExpDate - ls-MfgDate )
          IN ( %tky      = ls-%tky
               ValidDays = lv_days ) ).

    LOOP AT lt_products INTO DATA(ls_product).
      IF ls_product-ExpDate <= ls_product-MfgDate.
        APPEND VALUE #(
          %tky = ls_product-%tky
          %msg = new_message_with_text(
                   severity = if_abap_behv_message=>severity-error
                   text     = 'Expiry Date must be after Manufacturing Date!' )
        ) TO reported-znk_product_i.
      ENDIF.
    ENDLOOP.
    READ ENTITIES OF znk_product_I IN LOCAL MODE
                                   ENTITY znk_product_I
                                   ALL FIELDS
                                   WITH CORRESPONDING #( keys )
                                   RESULT DATA(lt_result).

    result = VALUE #( FOR ls IN lt_result
                      ( %tky   = ls-%tky
                        %param = ls ) ).   

  ENDMETHOD.
 

Important RAP-specific ABAP concepts

READ ENTITIES — The RAP-specific way to read data from a BO. Always use this inside behavior implementations — never use SELECT directly.

MODIFY ENTITIES — The RAP-specific way to change data inside behavior implementations — never use MODIFY dbtab directly.

IN LOCAL MODE — Bypasses authorization checks and feature controls when called from within the same BO's implementation. Important for internal BO operations.

%tky — The transactional key — a structure containing all key fields of the entity. Used to identify records throughout RAP's internal processing.

failed / reported — Standard output parameters for all RAP methods. Populate failed to signal which records errored. Populate reported to send messages back to the UI.

🌐Step 9 — Service Definition & Service Binding

Service Definition

Defines which CDS entities are exposed and under what names:

@EndUserText.label: 'Service Definition for Consumption view'
define service Znk_sd_product {
  expose znk_product_c;
}
 

Service Binding

The Service Binding ties a Service Definition to a specific protocol and usage type. For Fiori apps, you create an OData V4 binding with type UI:

  • Binding Type: OData V4 - UI
  • Activate the binding to get the OData service URL
  • Use "Preview" in ADT to open the Fiori Elements app directly

Once activated, your Product BO is fully functional as a Fiori Elements List Report + Object Page app — with list, filter, create, edit, draft, save, and all your custom actions.

💡Key Takeaways

The Purpose of Each Layer — Summary

DATABASE TABLE     → Where data lives permanently
DRAFT TABLE        → Where in-progress data lives temporarily
INTERFACE VIEW     → Clean data model, service-agnostic, reusable
CONSUMPTION VIEW   → Service-specific window — what this app sees
METADATA EXTENSION → UI layout — how fields look in Fiori
BASE BDEF          → All possible BO operations defined
PROJECTION BDEF    → Subset of operations for this specific service
BAP CLASS          → Custom business logic — validations, actions
SERVICE DEFINITION → Which entities go into the OData service
SERVICE BINDING    → Which protocol (OData V4) and port (UI/API)
 

The Two-Layer Pattern (Interface + Consumption) — Why it matters

The separation of Interface and Consumption layers is the most important design decision in RAP. It gives you:

  1. Reusability — one BO, multiple services (UI service, API service, integration service)
  2. Flexibility — each service exposes exactly what it needs
  3. Stability — changing the UI doesn't break the underlying BO contract
  4. Extensibility — SAP's own S/4HANA BOs follow this same pattern

Managed vs Unmanaged at a glance

In this managed scenario, the RAP framework wrote all the database interaction code for you. You only wrote:

  • Validation logic (validateDates)
  • Determination logic (setInitialStatus)
  • Action logic (checkProductValidity, Clear)

Everything else — INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, draft handling, locking, ETag — was handled by the framework automatically.

Github Link :  RAP-Managed-in-SAP 

Thanks,

Naveen Kumar SAP ABAP Developer | BTP Explorer

entry.title: No user exit for that SAP screen? Check who at SAP already enhanced it
entry.content:
This morning a question came in on Q&A: in VA01 and VA02, how do I make the partner function and the partner number read-only on the Partner tab, without modifying LV09CF63? Is there a user exit or a BAdI?

Maybe yes... maybe not. Sandra Rossi had already given the right first step in the thread: read what happens between LOOP WITH CONTROL and ENDLOOP. I did that, and then one more thing that I want to share here, because it works for almost any "is there an exit for this screen?" question.

Step one: search the whole function group, not only the include

The partner tab is screen 1000 of function group V09C. The include from the question, LV09CF63, has FORM SETUP_TC_FIELDS_1000, which does LOOP AT SCREEN and MODIFY SCREEN once per partner line. Nothing to plug into there.

So I searched all 120 includes of V09C on S/4HANA 2023 for the usual suspects: CUSTOMER-FUNCTION, USEREXIT, GET BADI, CALL BADI, ENHANCEMENT-POINT and ENHANCEMENT-SECTION.

Zero classic user exits. One BAdI, BADI_SD_DOC_BP_ADDR_CHECK, but it only decides if the partner address can be changed. And three explicit enhancement points, all in enhancement spot ES_SAPLV09C:

  • IS_ENHANCEMENT_01_01, alone inside PBO module IS_ENHANCEMENT_01 of screen 1000 (include LV09CO01)
  • EHP_LV09CF30_01, in FORM SET_TC_DATA_1000
  • section LV09CF33_01, in FORM USER_COMMAND_1000

The first one looks promising: a PBO module of the screen with nothing in it but an enhancement point. But looking promising is not proof. Does it run once per line, inside the table control loop, or once for the whole screen?

Step two: ask who at SAP already used it

This is the part I like. In ADT, a where-used on include LV09CO01 doesn't only show code. It also lists the enhancement implementations hanging on the program. For V09C there were four, all from SAP:

  • OIG_SAPLV09C_01 (IS-Oil)
  • OIG_LV09CF33_01 (IS-Oil)
  • VPD_SFWS_SC1_V09C_SET_TC_DATA
  • /ACCGO/ACM_EI_TC_DISBL_PARTNER, described as "Enhancement to Disable Partner for Closed Status of Trading Contract"

Read that last description again. SAP's own Agricultural Contract Management needed the same thing the person in the question needed.

To know which point each one implements, table ENHINCINX helps. With PROGRAMNAME = 'SAPLV09C' it returned OIG_SAPLV09C_01 on \PR:SAPLV09C\EX:IS_ENHANCEMENT_01_01. Exactly our point.

Step three: read their code

The IS-Oil implementation has 179 lines, and one block in it is the requirement from the question (I cut the IS-Oil specific condition around it):

loop at screen.
  if ( screen-name = 'GVS_TC_DATA-REC-PARVW' or
       screen-name = 'GVS_TC_DATA-REC-PARTNER' ) and
       gvs_tc_data-rec-parvw <> ' '.
    screen-input = 0.
    modify screen.
  endif.
endloop.

It reads GVS_TC_DATA-REC-PARVW, the partner of the current line, and changes the screen fields of that line. So the module runs inside the loop, once per partner. That answered my "once per line or once per screen" doubt better than any guess, and it came with a template ready to copy.

One more detail from the same code. To know where it is running, the implementation reads data of the calling program with a dynamic ASSIGN: assign ('(SAPMOIGS)T180') to <fs_t180>. The partner screen doesn't know the order header, so if your rule depends on it (for example, only orders created with reference), the same trick gives you '(SAPMV45A)VBAK' in VA01 and VA02. It's not a released interface, and SAP's own code lives with that risk too.

What surprised me most: the answer was not in the include everybody looks at. It was in the where-used list, in objects SAP itself wrote for its industry solutions.

Two things before you code

First, check if you need code at all. SETUP_TC_FIELDS_1000 reads TPAER from the partner determination procedure (VOPA). "No change possible" (AENDB) locks the partner number once it is filled, and "Partner mandatory" (PAPFL) locks the partner function. If your rule is fixed per partner function and order type, customizing already does it. Just not in the standard procedure: in my system 170 order types share procedure TA, so I would copy it to a Z procedure and assign that only to the order type that needs the lock.

Second, what I didn't do. Two of the four implementations came back empty when I tried to read them (the /ACCGO one and the VPD one), and I didn't dig into why. The point and the module are the same in S/4HANA 2025. And I didn't run VA02 with an implementation of my own: if you do, tell me what you see.

If you have your own trick for "is there an exit for this screen?", I would like to hear it in the comments.

entry.title: AI‑Guided Desired Vendor in ME51N — explainable supplier recommendation in the Purchase Requisition
entry.content:
A custom SAP S/4HANA AI use case, built responsibly on SAP BTP + SAP AI Core.

Part 1 of 3 — "AI‑Guided Supplier Selection in SAP S/4HANA". This part: the in‑transaction assistant. Part 2: the SAP BTP + AI Core "brain". Part 3: the standalone RAP + Fiori app. (Prototype / proof‑of‑concept — a custom extension, not standard/embedded functionality. System IDs, hostnames and deployment IDs are masked.)

Prerequisites (prototype). Part 1 needs SAP S/4HANA (ABAP Platform) with the classic ME_PROCESS_REQ_CUST BAdI.
